introduction_markdown:
**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 3 (0760), Paper 3 - Africa and World History, ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections (Section A: Africa, 1800-1945; Section B: Africa, 1945 to the present; Section C: World Revolutions and Diplomacy, 1700-1919; Section D: World, 1919 to the present date). All questions carry equal marks (25 marks each).

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown: **SECTION D: WORLD, 1919 TO THE PRESENT DATE**
incertitudes: Règle de choix : le sujet impose « answer FOUR questions, choosing ONE from each of the four sections ». `regles_choix` porte une règle « 1 sur 3 » par section (A, B, C, D), ce qui correspond exactement à la consigne imprimée ; la consigne complète est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question porte 25 marks imprimés (« All questions carry equal marks »), soit 100 points pour les quatre questions à traiter. Aucun écart de points constaté ; `points` vaut 25 pour l'exercice et pour l'unique question de chaque fichier.

Sujet scanné de deux pages (page de garde et questions 1 à 12) ; filigranes gcerevision ignorés. Le texte de la page 2 transparaît en miroir sur la page de garde (verso mal opacifié) et quelques espaces sont manquants à l'impression (question 8 : « between1871and1890 », rétabli en « between 1871 and 1890 ») ; aucune question coupée ni illisible, aucune figure ni carte dans le sujet.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées au niveau Advanced Level (introduction, développement, conclusion argumentée). Aucune citation n'est inventée et les chiffres sont limités à des repères datés de l'historiographie courante (dates, traités) ; à relire par un historien avant mise en vente.

Question 4 : l'énoncé imprimé date le déclenchement de la révolte Mau Mau de 1951. L'historiographie situe la montée de la violence en 1950-52 (mouvement interdit en août 1950, état d'urgence proclamé le 20 octobre 1952) ; le sujet est recopié tel quel et le corrigé précise la chronologie sans corriger l'énoncé.

Question 5 : l'Afrique équatoriale française regroupe le Gabon, le Moyen-Congo, l'Oubangui-Chari et le Tchad ; le Cameroun, ancien mandat puis tutelle, n'en faisait pas partie. Les interventions militaires françaises (Gabon 1964, Tchad à partir de la fin des années 1960, Centrafrique 1979) et le rôle du réseau Foccart sont cités selon l'historiographie courante, sans chiffres.

Question 7 : le sujet emploie « romanisation » au sens de la promotion du catholicisme romain par Jacques II ; les dates de 1688 sont données en style ancien (naissance du prince le 10 juin, acquittement des sept évêques et invitation à Guillaume le 30 juin, débarquement à Torbay le 5 novembre).

Question 9 : le montant des réparations (132 milliards de marks-or, fixé en 1921) et les pertes territoriales sont cités de mémoire historique établie ; aucune statistique de population n'est avancée.

Question 11 : la Banque mondiale et le FMI sont des institutions spécialisées de l'ONU ; l'UNICEF (fonds et non institution spécialisée) n'est volontairement pas traité. Les dates (variole déclarée éradiquée en 1980, Alma-Ata 1978, convention 182 de l'OIT en 1999, Codex Alimentarius 1963, retrait des États-Unis de l'UNESCO en 1984-85) sont citées selon l'historiographie courante.

Question 12 : le sujet vise la rupture sino-soviétique après la mort de Staline (1953). Les dates (discours de Khrouchtchev en février 1956, rupture de l'accord nucléaire en 1959, retrait des conseillers en 1960, congrès de Bucarest en juin 1960, guerre sino-indienne 1962, incidents de l'Oussouri en mars 1969) sont données selon l'historiographie courante ; aucun chiffre n'est avancé.

Thèmes : les noms sont qualifiés pour éviter les collisions avec les Tags de l'Histoire francophone (`sino-soviet split`, `afrikaner nationalism`, `mau mau revolt in kenya`...) ; plusieurs sont réutilisés des sujets History 2020-2021 (`scramble for africa`, `apartheid in south africa`, `cold war`, `indirect rule in colonial africa`) ; à revérifier à l'ingestion avec `find_tag_variant`.

questions.enonce_markdown:
To what extent was the outbreak of the Second World War a consequence of Hitler's aggressions?

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The Second World War in Europe began on 1 September 1939, when Germany invaded Poland, and Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September. Adolf Hitler, Chancellor from January 1933, followed a policy of rearmament, revision of the Treaty of Versailles and expansion to the east. The question asks how far the war was a consequence of his aggressions. The argument is that Hitler's aggressive aims and actions were the immediate and most important cause, but that his success depended on conditions created by the weaknesses of the League of Nations, the policy of appeasement, the effects of the First World War peace settlement and the Great Depression, and by the aggression of other powers.

**1. Hitler's aggressions (the main cause).**
- *Breaking the Treaty of Versailles step by step.* Germany left the Disarmament Conference and the League of Nations in October 1933, announced conscription and an air force in March 1935 (in the Anglo-German Naval Agreement of June 1935 Britain accepted a German fleet, which showed that Versailles was being set aside), and remilitarised the Rhineland in March 1936.
- *Expansion.* The Anschluss with Austria (March 1938), the demand for and occupation of the Sudetenland after the Munich Agreement (September-October 1938), the occupation of the rest of Bohemia and Moravia (March 1939) and of Memel (March 1939) showed that his aims went beyond the revision of the treaty to the domination of Europe and the search for *Lebensraum* ("living space") in the east.
- *Poland.* In 1939 Hitler demanded Danzig and a route across the Corridor. After Britain and France guaranteed Polish independence (31 March 1939), he secured his eastern flank by the Nazi-Soviet Pact of 23 August 1939 and invaded Poland, expecting that Britain and France would not act. This invasion was the direct cause of the outbreak of war.
- *Aims.* The plans recorded in documents such as the Hossbach Memorandum (1937, whose use by historians is debated) and his own writings suggest that he was ready for war.

**2. Other factors.**
- *The weaknesses of the League of Nations and collective security.* The League failed to stop Japan in Manchuria (1931) and Italy in Abyssinia (1935-36), so aggression was seen to succeed, and the great powers failed to cooperate (the USA was outside, Britain and France were divided).
- *Appeasement.* Britain and France, tired by the First World War, afraid of bombing and not ready in rearmament, accepted German violations, notably in the Rhineland, Austria and Czechoslovakia (Munich), believing that his claims were reasonable. This encouraged him to go further. The policy also reflected sympathy for the argument that Versailles had been unfair.
- *The Treaty of Versailles and the Depression.* Resentment of the treaty and the economic crisis of 1929-33 helped the Nazis to gain power; the Depression also made other states concentrate on their own problems.
- *Other aggressors and alliances.* Italian and Japanese expansion, the Rome-Berlin Axis (1936), the Anti-Comintern Pact (1936) and the Spanish Civil War (1936-39) made the international situation more dangerous. Stalin's deal with Hitler in 1939, after Britain and France failed to form a firm alliance with the USSR, freed Hitler from the threat of a two-front war.
- *The USA's isolationism and the weakness of France.* The USA's Neutrality Acts and France's defensive military strategy limited resistance.

**3. Evaluation.** Historians differ. Many place primary responsibility on Hitler's programme. A. J. P. Taylor (*The Origins of the Second World War*, 1961) argued that Hitler was more an opportunist who took advantage of the mistakes of others, which reduces his responsibility, but this view is disputed because of the evidence of his aims and of the way he prepared for war with Poland. It is clear that Hitler's actions were necessary for the war, but not sufficient: they succeeded because of the passive or divided response of the other powers.

**Conclusion.** To a very large extent the outbreak of the Second World War was a consequence of Hitler's aggression, since he actively sought a war of expansion and forced it by invading Poland. However, it was also the result of the failure of collective security, the policy of appeasement, the consequences of the First World War and the Great Depression, which created the conditions in which his aggression could succeed.
